title: She Wasn't Trying to Get Rid of Ruth: The Heartbreaking Reason Naomi Told Her to Go Home
paragraphs:
She Wasn't Trying to Get Rid of Ruth: The Heartbreaking Reason Naomi Told Her to Go Home
The Moment That Looks Like Rejection Was Actually One of the Most Selfless Acts in Scripture
There are moments in life when someone loves you so deeply that they are willing to let you walk away.
Not because they do not care.
Not because they have stopped believing in you.
But because they genuinely believe you deserve something better than what they can give.
That is the painful scene unfolding in the Book of Ruth.
Many people read Naomi's words and assume she was pushing Ruth away.
At first glance, it certainly looks that way.
A grieving widow tells her daughter-in-law to return home.
Yet beneath those tears lies one of the most misunderstood acts of sacrificial love in all of Scripture.
To understand why Naomi told Ruth to return home, we must first understand what Naomi had lost.
Naomi, whose name means "pleasant" in Hebrew, left Bethlehem during a famine with her husband Elimelech and their two sons.
They traveled to Moab seeking survival.
Then her sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth.
After about ten years, both sons died as well.
When Scripture describes Naomi returning to Bethlehem, she is not walking home victorious.
The Hebrew text captures her anguish powerfully.
"Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara."
"For the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me."
This is not the language of a woman who has everything figured out.
This is the language of someone trying to survive heartbreak.
As Naomi prepares to return to Bethlehem, she turns to Ruth and Orpah and says:
The Hebrew verb שׁוּב (shuv) means "to return," "to go back," or "to turn around."
She repeats this command multiple times.
She was trying to protect them.
In the ancient Near East, this was not merely unfortunate.
A woman without family protection often faced poverty and vulnerability.
Naomi knows exactly what awaits her in Bethlehem.
And she refuses to drag Ruth and Orpah into that suffering.
Not because she does not love them.
Real love is willing to sacrifice companionship for another person's good.
"Have I yet sons in my womb, that they may become your husbands?"
Under Israel's levirate marriage customs, a deceased man's brother could marry the widow to preserve the family line.
"I have nothing left to offer you."
At least, that is how she sees it.
What makes this scene even more emotional is that Naomi is not thinking about herself.
Naomi is willing to be alone.
Because Naomi believes Ruth deserves a better life than the one she can provide.
How many parents have done that?
She returns to her family, culture, and homeland.
There is no condemnation in the text.
But Ruth does something that still echoes through history.
Her words remain among the most beautiful declarations of loyalty ever spoken:
"But Ruth said, 'Do not urge me to leave you.'"
"For where you go I will go."
"And where you stay I will stay."
This is not merely loyalty to Naomi.
Ruth is not simply choosing a mother-in-law.
She is choosing the God of Israel.
She is leaving everything familiar behind.
Her future as she understood it.
She is stepping into uncertainty because she believes the God Naomi serves is worth following.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Many of us know what it feels like to stand where Ruth stood.
To trust God when the future makes no sense.
To walk by faith rather than sight.
To follow Christ without knowing where the road leads.
That is why Ruth's story continues to move hearts thousands of years later.
Because it is ultimately a picture of discipleship.
"Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me."
Ruth embodies that principle centuries before Bethlehem would welcome another unexpected visitor.
Naomi thinks she is returning empty.
But God is already writing redemption.
Naomi thinks her story is ending.
God knows it is just beginning.
That child becomes part of a lineage leading directly to King David.
And generations later, to Jesus Christ Himself.
A woman many people would have overlooked.
Yet God places her in the family line of the Messiah.
This is the Gospel hidden within Ruth.
God specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
Perhaps that is why this story still captures the human heart.
Because many of us feel more like Naomi than we would like to admit.
Moments where we looked at our lives and quietly wondered whether God had forgotten us.
Yet the entire book proves something astonishing.
Even when God's hand seems invisible, His providence remains active.
Even when we cannot see Him working, He is.
Even when the chapter feels painful, the Author has not abandoned the story.
The Greek New Testament later captures this same truth through Paul's words:
But God works through all things for good for those who love Him.
And perhaps it is your story too.
Maybe you are standing in the middle of a chapter that makes no sense.
She thought she was returning with nothing.
Yet she was unknowingly walking beside a woman who would become part of the lineage of Jesus Christ.
The blessing was already walking next to her.
She just could not see it yet.
Someone you know may be carrying a Naomi-sized burden and desperately need this reminder today.
Have you ever felt like Naomi?
Have you ever walked by faith like Ruth?
Your support helps us create and share more Gospel-centered content that reaches the hurting, strengthens believers, and proclaims biblical truth in a world desperate for hope.
The chapter that feels empty today may be the very chapter God uses to introduce the miracle you cannot yet see.
